passage: I'm Rekha, Charu's big sister, and I've noticed my sister has started doing a new thing. When she comes home from school, before she even takes off her shoes, she tells us everyone's marks. "Riddhi got 19, Bunty got 15, I got 17. So I'm third." Yesterday she won a medal in the drawing competition and bounced around the house all evening. Today she came home silent. When I asked, she said, "Anaya's drawing got put on the main board. Mine only went on the class board." Same drawing, same medal. She went from the happiest person in the house to someone sitting on the stairs pulling at her socks. I don't know what's going on inside her head. But I don't think it's the drawing she's measuring.

qa.q: What did Charu win yesterday?
qa.a: A medal in the drawing competition.

qa.q: Why might Charu have come home silent today, with the same medal?
qa.a: Seeing Anaya's drawing on the main board made her feel small, as if her worth depended on where she ranked.

qa.q: How could Rekha support Charu on the stairs?
qa.a: Rekha could sit with her and ask what she likes about her own drawing, drawing her attention back from the rankings to the work itself.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents feel hearing everyone's marks before her shoes are even off?
qa.a: They might be amused at first, then worried that Charu measures herself so much against others.

grounding: An older sister watches a child track classmates' marks and prizes, swinging between pride and feeling small depending on her rank.

passage:
Tuesday. The science tests came back. Tejas had 14 out of 20 and immediately craned to see Vinita's paper: 19. His ears went hot. He turned his paper face down and didn't speak at lunch.
Friday. At sports day, Tejas came first in the sack race. He counted: three medals for Vinita last year, one for him now. Still behind, he thought, but he walked a little taller.
The next Wednesday. Instead of only checking Vinita's mark, Tejas asked her how she'd answered the question about plant cells. "I draw it first, then label," she said, showing him. He tried it on the homework and got the diagram right. That evening, though, he still wrote in the back of his notebook: Vinita 19, me 14. He looked at it for a while, then drew a small plant cell next to it.

qa.q: What did Vinita score in the science test?
qa.a: 19 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel on Tuesday after seeing Vinita's paper?
qa.a: He felt small and embarrassed, which is why his ears went hot and he turned his paper face down.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday turned comparing into something useful?
qa.a: Asking Vinita how she answered the plant-cell question and trying her method, so the comparison helped him learn.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Tejas asking about her method?
qa.a: Vinita might feel pleased and happy to help, unaware that Tejas had been keeping score of her marks.

grounding: Over a week a child ranks himself against a classmate, feeling small or proud, and begins to use the comparison to learn.

passage: Charu, you're upset because Meenu got more stars than you? Sit here with your Rekha nani. When I was ten, I kept a list in my head of every girl in my class: who wrote neater, who sang better, who had shinier shoes. When I came first, I walked home like a queen. When Sudha beat me in sums, I wouldn't eat my dinner. My mother used to say, "Rekha, you are only as happy as your last rank." It was true. Then one day our teacher put my old copy from the start of the year beside my new one. So much better! I hadn't even noticed, because I was only ever looking at Sudha. Looking at others can tell you where you are, beta. Just don't let it tell you who you are.

qa.q: What did young Rekha's teacher put side by side?
qa.a: Rekha's old copy from the start of the year and her new one.

qa.q: What did young Rekha feel when Sudha beat her in sums?
qa.a: She felt so small and upset that she wouldn't eat her dinner.

qa.q: What could Charu try, instead of counting Meenu's stars?
qa.a: Charu could compare today's work with earlier work, as Rekha nani's teacher showed her, to see real progress.

qa.q: How might Rekha nani's mother have felt watching her daughter's moods rise and fall with each rank?
qa.a: She probably worried, which is why she told Rekha she was only as happy as her last rank.

grounding: A grandmother recalls ranking herself against classmates as a child, her self-worth rising and falling with each comparison.

passage: The drawing competition was in a school hall so noisy with parents and loudspeakers that Gurleen could barely think. Twenty minutes left. Gurleen liked her river, until she glanced at Gopika's paper: a whole village, with tiny goats. Suddenly her river looked thin. She looked again. And again. Each time, Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse. Ten minutes left, and only half her sky was coloured. Gopika won a certificate; Gurleen got nothing. On the way home she said, "I'm bad at drawing." Papa said, "Last week you told me you were the best in class." Gurleen thought. "That was when I only saw Nimmi's."

qa.q: How much time was left when Gurleen first glanced at Gopika's paper?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel each time she looked at Gopika's drawing?
qa.a: She felt smaller each time; Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse, though she had liked her river before.

qa.q: What went wrong during the competition, and what could Gurleen try next time?
qa.a: Checking Gopika's paper again and again used up her time, so half the sky stayed blank; next time she could keep her eyes on her own river until the end.

qa.q: How might Papa see Gurleen's two opposite claims about her drawing?
qa.a: Papa can see that her opinion of herself swings with whoever she compares against, so the ranking, not the drawing, is shaping how she feels.

grounding: A child keeps checking a classmate's drawing during a noisy competition and feels smaller each time, showing how constant ranking colours self-worth.

passage: In the Pune housing society's skating class, every child had a sticker chart. Mahima checked everyone's before she even tied her skates. Eshaan: four stickers. Hers: six. She skated faster that evening, grinning. On Thursday a new girl, Sia, arrived with ten stickers from her old class. Mahima's legs felt heavy. She fell twice and told the coach she had a tummy ache. Walking home past the vegetable carts, Eshaan asked, "Why are you sad? You learnt the turn today." Mahima blinked. She had forgotten the turn completely. "I did, na?" She tried it again on the society path, wobbling, and laughed.

qa.q: How many stickers did Sia have?
qa.a: Ten stickers, from her old class.

qa.q: Why did Mahima tell the coach she had a tummy ache?
qa.a: She felt small and deflated after seeing Sia's ten stickers, and wanted a way out of skating while she felt like that.

qa.q: What turning point did Eshaan's question create for Mahima?
qa.a: By reminding her she learnt the turn today, Eshaan helped her notice her own progress instead of the sticker count, and she happily tried it again 🙂

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about being counted against Mahima's chart?
qa.a: With four stickers, Eshaan might feel ranked below her, yet he still noticed her progress kindly, which suggests he wasn't keeping score the same way.

grounding: A child ranks friends by skating stickers and feels proud or small by turns, until a friend's question points her back to her own progress.

passage: In class five, I spent more time looking at Kamal's paper than my own. When the teacher returned tests, I'd peep at his mark first. If I'd beaten him, I felt ten feet tall. If he'd beaten me, I felt tiny, even if I'd got eighty-five. I did the same with drawings, sports day ribbons, even how many stars we got in our notebooks. It helped a bit: I knew where I stood, and I worked harder in maths because of him. But slowly, I stopped enjoying anything unless I'd won. One day, Kamal got a prize for a poem, and I felt sick, although I didn't even like writing poems. My mother asked why I was sad. I couldn't explain. I'm Nazia, and looking back, I'd tied my whole mood to a boy who didn't even know I was counting.

qa.q: What prize did Kamal get?
qa.a: Kamal got a prize for a poem.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel when Kamal beat Nazia in a test?
qa.a: Nazia felt tiny and deflated, even after scoring well, because the comparison set the mood.

qa.q: What could help Nazia keep the useful side of comparing?
qa.a: Nazia could use comparison to learn, like working harder in maths, while also noticing personal progress and enjoying tasks for their own sake.

qa.q: How might Kamal have seen their class five year?
qa.a: Kamal probably didn't know Nazia was counting and just got on with his own work.

grounding: A child looks back on checking a classmate's marks and prizes, feeling proud or small by ranking, and seeing how constant comparison coloured self-worth.

passage:
Art teacher's note, Thursday.
Kiran (class four) has started checking everyone's drawings before starting their own. Today, when Vaibhav held up a bright elephant, Kiran looked at their own sketch, crumpled it and said, "Mine's rubbish." Last week, when Kiran's painting was put on the board above Vaibhav's, Kiran grinned all day and told everyone. Comparing seems to help Kiran see what good work looks like, but it's starting to decide how Kiran feels about everything. I sat with Kiran and asked what they liked about their own drawing before it was crumpled. Kiran said, "The trees." I suggested keeping a folder of their drawings so they can see their own progress over the year. We'll start tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav hold up?
qa.a: Vaibhav held up a bright elephant.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when crumpling the sketch?
qa.a: Kiran felt small and discouraged, judging the drawing only against Vaibhav's.

qa.q: Why is the folder idea helpful?
qa.a: It lets Kiran compare with their own past work, keeping the useful side of comparison without constant ranking against others.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel seeing Kiran crumple the sketch?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel confused or awkward, not wanting a drawing to make a friend feel bad.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who checks others' drawings and feels proud or small by ranking, and helps the child track personal progress instead.

passage:
Saturday
Sports day. I got a silver in the sack race and a bronze in the relay. I was SO happy. Then I saw Yash had three golds. Three! Suddenly my medals looked like tin.
In class I always check his marks too. If I'm higher, I feel like a queen. If he's higher, I don't want to eat my tiffin.
Mummy saw me sulking and asked what's wrong. I told her. She said, "Last year you didn't win any medals. This year two. Who beat last year's Deepika?" I said, "Me." She said, "So why are you looking at Yash?"
I don't know. Maybe because he's there and last year's me isn't.
I put the silver on my shelf anyway. It's still shiny.
- Deepika

qa.q: How many golds did Yash win?
qa.a: Yash had three golds.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel after seeing Yash's golds?
qa.a: Deepika felt deflated, as if the medals were tin, even though a moment before she was very happy.

qa.q: What did Mummy help Deepika see?
qa.a: Mummy helped Deepika compare with last year's self, which shows progress instead of feeling small next to Yash.

qa.q: How might Yash see sports day?
qa.a: Yash is probably just enjoying his golds, unaware that Deepika was measuring her day against his.

grounding: A child checks a classmate's medals and marks, feeling proud or small by ranking, and a parent helps her compare with her own past instead.

passage:
At the village school's drawing competition, the teacher pinned all the pictures on the wall. Mahima ran to see.
Her mango tree had got a star. Nandini's peacock had two stars. Mahima's tummy sank. Then she saw that the boy next to her had no stars at all, and she felt a little better.
All afternoon she kept looking. Who had more? Who had less? She counted the stars twice.
Walking home past the fields, Nandini said, "I liked your mango tree. The leaves looked real."
Mahima was quiet. She had been so busy counting stars, she hadn't really looked at anyone's drawing, not even her own.

qa.q: How many stars did Nandini's peacock get?
qa.a: Nandini's peacock had two stars.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when she saw the boy with no stars?
qa.a: She felt a little better, because being above someone made her feel less small.

qa.q: What could Mahima try at the next competition?
qa.a: She could look at what she likes in each drawing, including her own, instead of only counting stars.

qa.q: How does Nandini seem to see Mahima's drawing?
qa.a: Nandini sees it warmly, admiring how the leaves looked real, without comparing stars.

grounding: Shows a child checking classmates' drawings and feeling proud or small by comparison, until ranking crowds out enjoying the work.

passage:
In Tel Aviv, Yosef's class got back their spelling tests. Yosef had eighteen out of twenty. He grinned, then leaned to look at Olga's paper. Twenty. Olga was already folding hers away.
His grin disappeared. He checked the boy behind him. Fifteen. He grinned again.
At home he said, "I'm third best, Mum. Or maybe fourth. Olga got twenty."
"What did you get?"
"Eighteen."
"Last month you got twelve."
Yosef stopped. He had forgotten about last month.
"Are you proud of eighteen?" his mother asked.
He thought. "Only if nobody's better."
His mother raised her eyebrows. Yosef frowned at his own answer.

qa.q: What did Yosef get on the spelling test?
qa.a: Yosef had eighteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why did Yosef's grin disappear when he saw Olga's paper?
qa.a: Seeing Olga's twenty made him feel smaller and less proud of his own mark.

qa.q: How did Yosef's mother help him?
qa.a: She reminded him that last month he got twelve, helping him see his own progress instead of only others' marks.

qa.q: How might Olga feel if she knew Yosef was checking her paper?
qa.a: Olga might feel uncomfortable or pressured, not wanting her marks to be someone else's measuring stick.

grounding: Shows a child whose pride rises and falls with classmates' marks, until a parent points to his own progress.

passage:
At the district sports club, the junior swimmers lined up for medals. Madhuri got bronze in freestyle. She held it up, beaming, until she saw Sarita's gold.
For the rest of the evening, she kept counting: Sarita, two golds. The girl from the other club, one silver. Me, one bronze. Every time someone passed with a medal, she checked its colour.
In the changing room, the coach asked, "Madhuri, how was your turn at the wall?"
"Slow. I only got bronze."
"Your turn was the best I've seen from you. Two seconds faster than last month."
Madhuri looked at the bronze again. It suddenly felt a little heavier, in a good way.

qa.q: What medal did Madhuri get in freestyle?
qa.a: She got bronze in freestyle.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she saw Sarita's gold?
qa.a: She felt her pride drop and felt smaller, comparing her bronze with Sarita's gold.

qa.q: How did the coach help Madhuri see her swim differently?
qa.a: The coach pointed to her own improvement, two seconds faster than last month, instead of the medal colours.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the evening?
qa.a: Sarita may simply be enjoying her golds, not knowing Madhuri is measuring herself against them.

grounding: Shows a child checking others' medals and feeling proud or small accordingly, and a coach helping her see her own progress.

passage: Before: At the Diwali drawing contest, Vasudha peeked at every paper on the wall. Omkar's rangoli drawing had a first-prize star. Hers had nothing. She felt small all evening. During: A week later, their maths tests came back. Vasudha got nineteen; Omkar got fourteen. She said loudly, "I beat Omkar!" and felt tall. Omkar looked at his desk. After: The next Monday, her Nani asked what she liked about her own drawing. Vasudha thought. "The lamp. I made the flame really glow." Nani smiled. "Then that's what counts." Vasudha still looked at the wall sometimes. But she also looked at her flame.

qa.q: What score did Vasudha get in the maths test?
qa.a: Nineteen.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when she said "I beat Omkar!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and tall, her mood rising because she ranked above someone else.

qa.q: What did Nani's question help Vasudha notice?
qa.a: It helped her notice what she liked in her own drawing, the glowing flame, instead of only comparing it with others.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar when Vasudha says she beat him?
qa.a: Omkar likely feels embarrassed and small, looking at his desk after being compared out loud.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose sense of worth rises and falls with how she compares to classmates.

passage: Nirmala, beta, come see this old box. You're upset because Rhea got more medals than you? Let me tell you about winter sports day when I was nine. I, your Pradeep Dadu, won one bronze for the sack race. I was so proud, I ran all the way home. Then I saw my neighbour's son with three golds on his coat. Suddenly my bronze looked like a bottle cap. I threw it in this very box and didn't look at it for years. Silly boy. That bronze was for my best race ever. Only later did I understand that measuring myself against him taught me where I stood, but it shouldn't have told me what I was worth.

qa.q: What race did Pradeep win bronze in?
qa.a: The sack race.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after seeing the neighbour's son's medals?
qa.a: He felt small and ashamed of his bronze, which suddenly looked like a bottle cap, though he had been proud a moment before.

qa.q: What choice in the story does Dadu regret?
qa.a: Throwing the bronze into the box and ignoring it for years, instead of valuing his best race.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's son have felt that day?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and happy, not knowing his three golds made young Pradeep feel small.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a child, comparing medals made him feel proud and then small.

passage: The power went out just as Class 5's term results were being read during the Holi week assembly, so the teacher shouted the marks in the dim hall. Disha strained to hear. "Afreen, ninety-two." Disha's heart sank; she had eighty-eight. She had been happy with it until one second ago. On the way back to class, she asked everyone their marks, one by one, keeping a list in her head. Above her: four. Below her: many. She felt a little better, then worse again. At home, Papa asked about the result. "I'm fifth," she said. "No, what did you get?" "Eighty-eight." "That's your best ever." Disha blinked. She hadn't thought of it that way at all.

qa.q: What mark did Afreen get?
qa.a: Ninety-two.

qa.q: Why did Disha's heart sink when she heard Afreen's mark?
qa.a: She suddenly felt disappointed and small, because her own eighty-eight seemed lower once she compared it.

qa.q: What could Disha try instead of asking everyone their marks?
qa.a: She could compare her mark with her own last result, as Papa did, to see real progress.

qa.q: How might Papa see Disha's answer "I'm fifth"?
qa.a: Papa seems surprised that she ranks herself rather than noticing her best ever score.

grounding: Illustrates a child ranking herself against classmates and feeling proud or small depending on the comparison.

passage: On the day after Sports Day in December, Kiran counted medals before the first bell. He had one silver, for the sack race. Suraj had two golds. Priyank had none at all. Kiran felt taller than Priyank and smaller than Suraj, both in the same minute. In art period he peeked at everyone's drawing of a winter tree before colouring his own. Suraj's tree had snow, somehow, in Mumbai. Kiran's tree suddenly looked flat. He rubbed it out. "Why did you do that?" asked Miss Joseph. "Suraj's is better." "I asked for your tree, not Suraj's," she said. At home, Kiran pinned the silver medal on his school bag, then took it off, then pinned it on again.

qa.q: Which race did Kiran win silver in?
qa.a: The sack race.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when he counted the medals?
qa.a: He felt proud next to Priyank and small next to Suraj, both in the same minute.

qa.q: What could help Kiran enjoy his own work more?
qa.a: He could look at his own tree before anyone else's and compare it with his earlier drawings, as Miss Joseph hinted 🙂.

qa.q: Why might Miss Joseph have said "I asked for your tree"?
qa.a: She wants Kiran to value his own effort instead of ranking himself against Suraj.

grounding: A child checks classmates' medals and drawings and feels proud or small by turns, letting the ranking colour his own work.
